title: 〜ながら（も） (contrast)
meaning: Expresses contrast: even though the first part is true, the second part is something that doesn't fit with it. Like “although ..., ...” or “even while ...”.
connection: Verb masu-stem／te-iru form・i-adjective dictionary form・na-adjective stem・noun + ながら（も）

senses.label: Even though (one knows)
senses.meaning: The first part is an ongoing state or awareness, yet the person does something that contradicts it. It often carries blame, regret, or self-mockery. 「〜ていながら」 and 「〜でありながら」 are very common.
senses.connection: Verb te-iru form + ながら（も）／noun + でありながら（も）; common: 「知っていながら」, 「分かっていながら」, 「知りながら」
examples: He knew what was going on, yet he said nothing.
I know it's bad for me, but I still end up smoking.
Even though he's a doctor, he doesn't care about his own health.

senses.label: Although ... still
senses.meaning: The first part is a quality or attribute, and the second part is an evaluation that goes against it, as in “small but ...” or “only a child, but ...”. It sounds fairly literary and often takes 「も」.
senses.connection: i-adjective dictionary form／na-adjective stem／noun + ながら（も）; e.g. 「狭いながらも」, 「小さいながらも」, 「子供ながら」
examples: Our home: small, but full of joy.
This shop is small, but it's always packed with customers.
He's just a child, but he has a mind of his own.

senses.label: Set phrases
senses.meaning: Fixed expressions used to open politely or to sound modest. They are courteous and common in greetings and letters.
senses.connection: 「残念ながら」, 「失礼ながら」, 「恐縮ながら」, 「陰ながら」, 「微力ながら」, 「我ながら」, etc.
examples: Unfortunately, I can't take part this time.
Excuse me, but may I ask your name?
I'm rooting for you from the sidelines.

notes: Verb masu-stem + ながら usually means “while doing”, so use context to tell whether it's contrastive. Adding 「も」 or using 「〜ていながら」 makes the contrast clear.
Both parts must have the same subject.
「生まれながら（に）」 and 「昔ながらの」 mean “as it was／unchanged” and are not contrastive.

daily.title: Making fun of yourself to a friend
daily.description: You did it even though you knew you shouldn't, with a bit of self-mockery.
daily.example: I knew I was on a diet, but I ate the cake anyway.

daily.title: Describing your home
daily.description: Modestly saying your place is small but comfortable.
daily.example: It's small, but it's a cozy room.

daily.title: Turning down an invitation
daily.description: Politely saying you can't come.
daily.example: Unfortunately, I have plans that day.

work.title: Thanking a client in a business email
work.description: Expressing modesty and support to a client.
work.example: I would be glad to help in whatever small way I can.

work.title: A news report about a company
work.description: Describing a company that is small but strong.
work.example: Although small, the company is known for its advanced technology.

etymology: 「ながら」 is generally thought to come from old 「な」 (like 「の」) + 「から（柄）」 meaning “nature, as it is”. Its original sense was “keeping the state of ...”. From “while staying in a state” it came to mean “while doing”, and then “although in that state, ...”.

similar.title: 〜のに
similar.explanation: 「のに」 carries strong feelings like frustration or surprise and is common in speech. 「ながら（も）」 is more objective and literary; the first part is usually a state, and the subject must be the same.

similar.title: 〜つつ（も）
similar.explanation: 「つつも」 also expresses contrast, but it only follows the verb masu-stem and is even more literary than 「ながらも」. 「ながらも」 can also follow adjectives and nouns.

similar.title: 〜ながら (simultaneous)
similar.explanation: The N5 「ながら」 means two actions happen at the same time (「音楽を聞きながら勉強する」). In the contrastive use, the first part is usually a state word.

similar.title: 〜ものの
similar.explanation: 「ものの」 also means “although”, focusing on “that's true, but what should follow didn't”. It often follows the ta-form. 「ながらも」 focuses on the clash between two states.

meaning: Since something happened in the past, a certain state has continued up to now. Like “ever since ...”.
connection: Verb te-form + 以来／noun + 以来

senses.label: Ever since ...
senses.meaning: A past action is the starting point, and the second part is a state that has continued from then on. The second part often uses 「ずっと」, 「〜ている」, or 「一度も〜ない」. Slightly formal.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + 以来; e.g. 「日本に来て以来」, 「卒業して以来」
examples: Ever since I came to Japan, I've lived in this town.
I haven't seen him even once since we graduated from college.

senses.label: Noun + 以来
senses.meaning: Same meaning after a noun for an event or point in time. 「それ以来」 and 「あれ以来」 refer back to what was said: “since then”.
senses.connection: Noun + 以来; e.g. 「入社以来」, 「先月以来」, 「それ以来」
examples: I haven't taken a single day off since I joined the company.
Since then, he has stopped drinking.

notes: The second part must be a continuing state or a repeated action, not a one-time action. ✕「日本に来て以来、富士山に登った」.
The starting point should be fairly far in the past. You don't say ✕「昨日来て以来」.
Compared with 「〜てから」, 「〜て以来」 stresses that something has continued from then until now.

daily.title: Catching up with a friend
daily.description: Talking about a habit you've kept since some change.
daily.example: Since I moved, I've been jogging every morning.

daily.title: Remembering an old classmate
daily.description: Saying you haven't been in touch for a long time.
daily.example: I haven't been in contact with her since we finished high school.

work.title: Introducing yourself
work.description: Describing your career at a meeting.
work.example: Since joining the company, I have been in charge of sales.

work.title: A news report
work.description: Reporting that a record or situation continues.
work.example: The highest temperature since records began was recorded.

etymology: 「以来」 is a word borrowed from Chinese. 「以」 means “from”, and 「来」 means “up to now”, so together they mean “from then until now”. In Japanese it follows the te-form and marks that action as the starting point.

similar.title: 〜てから
similar.explanation: 「てから」 just shows order (“after”), and the second part can be a one-time action. 「て以来」 stresses that something has continued from then until now.

similar.title: 〜てからというもの
similar.explanation: Similar meaning, but 「てからというもの」 stresses a big change from that point on. It is more emotional and literary.

title: 〜しかない (no choice but to)
meaning: There's no other way, so you have to do this. Like “have no choice but to ...” or “all you can do is ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + しかない

senses.label: Have no choice but to
senses.meaning: With no other option, you're forced to take a certain action. It sounds resigned.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + しかない／しかありません; often with 「〜から」 or 「〜なら」
examples: I missed the last train, so I have no choice but to take a taxi home.
The bus isn't coming, so we'll have to walk to the station.

senses.label: Making up your mind
senses.meaning: Since this is the only way, you resolve to do it. Also used to encourage others. Positive tone.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + しかない; common: 「やるしかない」, 「頑張るしかない」
examples: We've come this far, so we just have to do it.
If you want to pass, you just have to study every day.

notes: 「Noun + しかない」 means a small amount (「千円しかない」 = I only have 1,000 yen). That's the N5 「しか〜ない」, so don't mix them up.
More casual than 「〜ほかない」 or 「〜よりほかない」, and the most common in everyday speech.

daily.title: Before an exam
daily.description: Psyching yourself up.
daily.example: The exam is tomorrow. I'll just have to stay up all night.

daily.title: Something broke
daily.description: Talking with your family about what to do.
daily.example: If it can't be fixed, we'll just have to buy a new one.

work.title: A project behind schedule
work.description: A boss explains the situation to the team.
work.example: The deadline can't be changed, so we'll have to work overtime to deal with it.

etymology: 「しか」 is a limiting particle that pairs with a negative to mean “only”. 「〜するしかない」 literally means “there is nothing (no way) other than doing ...”, so “all you can do is ...”.

similar.title: 〜ほかない・〜よりほかない
similar.explanation: Same meaning, but more literary and formal. 「しかない」 is the most common in speech.

similar.title: 〜ざるを得ない
similar.explanation: Also means “have to”, but focuses on being forced by circumstances against your will. Literary.

similar.title: 〜しか〜ない (only)
similar.explanation: After a noun, it means a small amount or narrow range. This pattern follows the verb dictionary form and means there's no other choice.

meaning: Shows taking steps in advance to prevent something bad. Like “in case ...” or “so that ... doesn't happen”.
connection: Verb te-form + はいけないから／verb dictionary form + といけないから

senses.label: In case (te-form)
senses.meaning: The first part is the bad thing you're worried about, and the second part is the precaution. It isn't a prohibition; it means “it would be bad if ...”. In speech you can say 「〜ちゃいけないから」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + はいけないから／ちゃいけないから
examples: Let's take an umbrella in case it rains.
Keep warm when you sleep so you don't catch a cold.
I'll put it up high so the kids don't touch it.

senses.label: In case (dictionary form)
senses.meaning: 「〜といけないから」 means the same as above and is more common in daily life. You can also say 「〜といけないので」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + といけないから／といけないので
examples: I'll write it down in case I forget.
I left home early in case I was late.

senses.label: Polite version
senses.meaning: 「〜ては困るので」 and 「〜てはいけませんので」 sound more polite. Often used at work to remind someone.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + は困るので／はいけませんので
examples: Please check it once more, just to make sure there are no mistakes.
I'll put the documents in a folder so they don't get lost.

notes: The second part is the speaker's intention, a suggestion, or a precaution already taken.
「ないといけないから」 and 「なくてはいけないから」 mean “because I have to ...”, which is completely different.
The similar 「〜ないように」 expresses a purpose. The form is different, but they're often interchangeable: 「忘れないようにメモする」.

daily.title: Before going out
daily.description: A mother reminds her child to take something.
daily.example: Take a jacket in case it gets cold.

daily.title: Planning a trip
daily.description: Talking with a friend about booking early.
daily.example: Let's book early in case it fills up.

work.title: Reminding a coworker
work.description: Telling someone to save their data.
work.example: Please save often so you don't lose any data.

etymology: It comes from the prohibition 「〜てはいけない」 (“... is no good”) + 「から」 for a reason. Literally “because ... would be no good, ...”, which came to mean “in case ...”.

similar.title: 〜ないように
similar.explanation: 「ないように」 directly states a purpose: “so as not to ...”. 「てはいけないから」 gives the worry as a reason for a precaution, and is more conversational.

similar.title: 〜てはいけない
similar.explanation: On its own, it's a prohibition: “you must not ...”. Adding 「から」 turns it into the precaution meaning “in case ...”.

similar.title: 〜ことのないように
similar.explanation: Also means “so that ... doesn't happen”, but is very formal and used in notices and rules.

meaning: Asks a question or expresses doubt in a polite, soft way. Like “I wonder ...” or “Could it be that ...?”.
connection: Plain form (na-adjective・noun: な) + のでしょうか

senses.label: Asking politely
senses.meaning: Asking about the reason behind something you see, or checking something. Softer and more polite than 「〜んですか」. In speech also 「〜んでしょうか」.
senses.connection: Plain form + のでしょうか／んでしょうか
examples: Excuse me, does this train stop at Shinjuku?
Why isn't he coming, I wonder?

senses.label: Doubt／asking yourself
senses.meaning: You don't necessarily expect an answer. It shows the speaker's doubt or skepticism. Often used to raise a question in writing or speeches.
senses.connection: Plain form + のでしょうか; often with 「本当に」 or 「なぜ」
examples: Is this really okay?
Why do people dream?

senses.label: Asking permission politely
senses.meaning: Asking if you may do something. More humble and careful than 「〜てもいいですか」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + も（よろしい／いい）のでしょうか
examples: Would it be all right to park here?
Is it all right if I join, too?

notes: 「でしょうか」 is already a polite question. Adding 「の」 adds the sense of wanting to know the background or reason.
Nouns and na-adjectives need 「な」: 「学生なのでしょうか」, 「静かなのでしょうか」.
Softer than 「〜のですか」, but using it again and again with a superior can sound distant. Switch to 「〜でしょうか」 depending on the situation.

daily.title: Asking for directions at a station
daily.description: Politely asking a staff member.
daily.example: Does this bus go to the airport?

daily.title: Watching a news program
daily.description: The host poses a question to viewers.
daily.example: Why are young people losing interest in cars?

work.title: Checking with a client
work.description: Gently asking about the reason in an email.
work.example: May I ask if there is a reason for the change to your order?

work.title: Raising a concern in a meeting
work.description: Gently expressing worry about a plan.
work.example: Will this budget really be enough?

etymology: It's made of 「の（のだ）」 for explanation, 「でしょう」 (the polite form of 「だろう」), and the question particle 「か」. In other words, it's the polite version of 「のだろうか」.

similar.title: 〜のだろうか
similar.explanation: 「のだろうか」 is plain style, used when talking to yourself or in writing. 「のでしょうか」 is polite and used to ask others.

similar.title: 〜んですか
similar.explanation: 「んですか」 asks for a reason more directly. 「のでしょうか」 adds a guessing tone and is softer.

similar.title: 〜でしょうか
similar.explanation: 「でしょうか」 is simply a polite question. Adding 「の」 focuses more on the reason or situation behind it.

meaning: A written way of stating something, equal to 「だ」. Used in papers, newspapers, and explanatory writing.
connection: Noun／na-adjective stem + である; verb・i-adjective plain form + のである

senses.label: Written “is”
senses.meaning: Same meaning as 「だ」, but serious and objective. Used in papers, reports, editorials, and the narration of novels. Verbs and adjectives take 「のである」, which adds an explaining or emphatic tone.
senses.connection: Noun／na-adjective stem + である; plain form + のである
examples: I am a cat.
Water is the source of life.
That, precisely, is the problem.

senses.label: Linking two statements
senses.meaning: 「であり」 and 「であって」 link two statements in the middle of a sentence, like spoken 「で」. 「AでありBでもある」 means “is A and also B”.
senses.connection: Noun／na-adjective stem + であり（、）／であって
examples: He is a doctor and also a writer.
Tokyo is the capital of Japan and also its largest city.

senses.label: Guessing／speeches
senses.meaning: 「であろう」 is the written form of 「だろう」 and shows a guess. 「であります」 is used in speeches and addresses and sounds very formal.
senses.connection: Noun／plain form + であろう; noun + であります
examples: This problem will likely become even more serious.
This is the responsibility of all of us.

notes: The 「である」 style is one writing style, alongside the 「です・ます」 style and the 「だ」 style. Don't mix them in one text.
Verbs and i-adjectives can't attach directly: ✕「行くである」 ✕「高いである」. Say 「行くのである」, 「高いのである」.
It's almost never used in conversation, but you often hear 「〜であります」 in speeches.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: You often meet it in the narration of novels.
daily.example: It was the beginning of a long winter.

daily.title: Reading a newspaper editorial
daily.description: Editorials state opinions in the 「である」 style.
daily.example: Education is the very force that supports a nation's future.

work.title: Writing a paper
work.description: Stating your view in the conclusion of a paper.
work.example: From the above results, it can be said that the hypothesis is correct.

work.title: Writing a report
work.description: Describing the current situation objectively.
work.example: The aim of this project is to make operations more efficient.

etymology: It's made of the particle 「で」 + the verb of existence 「ある」, literally “exists as ...”. In speech, 「である」 gradually shortened to 「であ」 → 「だ」, while 「である」 itself survived in writing.

similar.title: 〜だ・〜です
similar.explanation: 「だ」 is casual spoken style, 「です」 is polite, and 「である」 is written plain style. All three state the same thing; only the style differs.

similar.title: 〜でございます
similar.explanation: 「でございます」 is the very polite form of 「です」, used when speaking to customers. 「である」 shows no respect; it only sounds written and serious.

meaning: Shows adjusting something to fit a standard or person, or being suited to it. Like “in time with ...”, “to match ...”, or “suited to ...”.
connection: Noun + に合わせて／に合わせた + noun／に合った + noun

senses.label: Adjusting to match
senses.meaning: The first part is the standard, and the action or content in the second part is made to match it. Often used for adjusting to a person, season, or need.
senses.connection: Noun + に合わせて; e.g. 「音楽に合わせて」, 「予算に合わせて」
examples: Let's dance to the music.
We change the menu to suit the season.
We'll suggest a plan to fit your budget.

senses.label: Suited to
senses.meaning: 「に合った + noun」 means something that fits or suits the first part. Often used with 「自分」, 「目的」, 「体質」, etc.
senses.connection: Noun + に合った + noun／noun + に合う
examples: I'm looking for a job that suits me.
Choose cosmetics that suit your skin.

senses.label: Setting／going along with
senses.meaning: As a predicate, 「〜に合わせる」 means setting something to a standard, or going along with someone else's plans.
senses.connection: Noun + に合わせる／に合わせます
examples: I set my watch by the station clock.
I decided to go along with his schedule.

notes: The 「に合う」 in 「間に合う」 (“to be in time”) is not this grammar.
「〜に合わせて」 focuses on actively adjusting to something; 「〜に応じて」 focuses on changing in response to a change.

daily.title: At karaoke
daily.description: Friends clap along to the beat.
daily.example: Clap your hands to the rhythm, okay?

daily.title: Buying shoes
daily.description: A clerk recommends shoes that fit.
daily.example: It's important to choose shoes that fit the shape of your feet.

daily.title: Making plans with a friend
daily.description: Fitting in with the other person's schedule.
daily.example: Okay, I'll go with whatever works for you.

work.title: Pitching to a client
work.description: Saying you'll tailor the service to their needs.
work.example: We will provide a system tailored to your company's needs.

work.title: A news report
work.description: Reporting steps timed to an event.
work.example: A new station opened in time for the Olympics.

etymology: 「合わせる」 is the transitive form of 「合う」 (“to fit, to match”) and means “to make things match”. 「に合わせて」 means “making it match ...”, which extends to “in line with” or “according to”.

similar.title: 〜に応じて
similar.explanation: 「に応じて」 means something changes depending on the first part (「能力に応じて給料が決まる」). 「に合わせて」 means actively adjusting to one standard.

similar.title: 〜に沿って
similar.explanation: 「に沿って」 means acting in line with a policy or plan without straying. 「に合わせて」 focuses on adjusting to match.

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: 「によって」 means “differs depending on ...” and objectively describes differences. 「に合わせて」 is a deliberate adjustment.

meaning: Follows a noun for people or things, meaning among people or things of the same kind or in the same relationship. Like “fellow ...” or “... with each other”.

senses.label: Among the same kind
senses.meaning: Between people who share the same nature or position. Often used to describe interactions and relationships.
senses.connection: Noun + 同士; e.g. 「隣同士」, 「友達同士」, 「似た者同士」
examples: Please discuss it with the person next to you.
They're two of a kind, so they probably get along.

senses.label: A certain relationship
senses.meaning: Both sides are in the same kind of relationship, such as lovers or enemies. Often in the form 「AとBは〜同士だ」.
senses.connection: Noun + 同士だ／同士の + noun; e.g. 「恋人同士」, 「敵同士」
examples: Those two are a couple.
Parents shouldn't interfere in fights between children.

senses.label: Things and things
senses.meaning: It can also be used for things of the same kind.
senses.connection: Noun + 同士; e.g. 「車同士」, 「同じ極同士」
examples: Like poles of a magnet repel each other.
There was a car-to-car accident at the intersection.

notes: 「同士」 only follows nouns for the same kind, meaning “both being ...”. ✕「先生と学生同士」.
「同志」 (“comrade, like-minded person”) is written differently and means something different. Don't confuse them.

daily.title: At school
daily.description: A teacher has students practice in pairs.
daily.example: Please pair up with the person sitting next to you.

daily.title: Talking about friends
daily.description: Saying two people became close.
daily.example: Since they had the same hobbies, they became friends right away.

work.title: Inside a company
work.description: Explaining cooperation between departments.
work.example: We need to strengthen cooperation between departments.

work.title: A news report
work.description: Reporting competition between companies.
work.example: Competition among major companies is getting fiercer.

etymology: 「同士」 was originally written 「同志」, meaning like-minded people, and later came to mean anyone of the same kind. In modern Japanese, the suffix is written 「同士」, while 「同志」 keeps the meaning “comrade”.

similar.title: 〜たち
similar.explanation: 「たち」 only marks the plural. 「同士」 stresses the relationship between those of the same kind.

similar.title: 〜間（かん）
similar.explanation: 「〜間」 follows two or more parties to mean “between” (「日中間」, 「企業間」), and they can be different kinds. 「同士」 requires the same kind.

meaning: Shows that something is equivalent to something else in conversion, correspondence, date, or family relation. Like “corresponds to ...” or “falls on ...”.

senses.label: Equivalent to
senses.meaning: Shows that something corresponds to something in another system. Used for conversions, comparing systems, translating words, etc.
senses.connection: Noun + に当たる／に当たります
examples: One dollar is about 150 yen.
Japan's Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology corresponds to China's Ministry of Education.

senses.label: Falls on (a date)
senses.meaning: Shows that a date happens to fall on a certain day or anniversary.
senses.connection: Date noun + に当たる
examples: Christmas falls on a Sunday this year.
Today is the anniversary of my father's death.

senses.label: Family relations
senses.meaning: Shows how someone is related to someone else.
senses.connection: Noun for a person + に当たる（人）
examples: He is my cousin.
Mr. Tanaka is the company president's nephew.

notes: 「当たる」 also means “to hit, to win (a prize), to be in the sun” (「ボールが頭に当たった」). That is not this grammar.
「〜にあたって」 and 「〜にあたり」 mean “on the occasion of ...”, which is a different grammar point.
「〜には当たらない」 means “there's no need to ...”, also a different grammar point.

daily.title: Explaining to a foreign friend
daily.description: Explaining a Japanese custom.
daily.example: Japan's Obon is an event that corresponds to China's Qingming Festival.

daily.title: Looking at a calendar
daily.description: Checking dates with your family.
daily.example: Next year, my birthday falls on a Saturday.

work.title: Translation work
work.description: Explaining to a coworker how words correspond.
work.example: This word corresponds to the English “deadline”.

work.title: A news report
work.description: Reporting a proportion in statistics.
work.example: This figure is about 30% of the total.

etymology: The basic meaning of 「当たる」 is “to hit, to strike”. From “exactly hitting a target” it came to mean “to correspond to” and “to fall on (a day)”.

similar.title: 〜にあたって
similar.explanation: 「にあたって」 means “on the occasion of ...” and follows important events. 「に当たる」 means “to correspond to”.

similar.title: 〜として
similar.explanation: 「として」 shows a role or status (“as ...”). 「に当たる」 shows what something is equivalent to in a comparison.

similar.title: 〜に相当する
similar.explanation: Same meaning, but 「に相当する」 is more literary and formal, often for converting amounts or values.

meaning: Shows that something is on the same level as the first item and can be mentioned alongside it. Like “along with ...” or “as famous as ...”.
connection: Noun + と並んで／と並ぶ + noun／と並び

senses.label: On a par with
senses.meaning: The first item is a well-known example, and the second is said to be just as important or famous. Used for evaluations.
senses.connection: Noun + と並んで; noun + と並ぶ + noun
examples: Like Nara, Kyoto is known as a city rich in history.
He is a great player on a par with Ichiro.

senses.label: Written linking form
senses.meaning: 「と並び」 is a written form that links clauses. Often used in news and explanatory writing to list things of equal standing.
senses.connection: Noun + と並び、〜
examples: Along with New York and London, Tokyo is one of the world's financial centers.

senses.label: Side by side (literal)
senses.meaning: The literal meaning: standing, sitting, or walking side by side with someone.
senses.connection: Noun (person) + と並んで + action
examples: I sat down next to my friend.

notes: The first item is usually something widely known and representative, used to highlight the standing of the second.
In 「AはBと並んで〜」, A and B are judged in the same direction, usually positively.

daily.title: Talking about sports
daily.description: Discussing popular sports with a friend.
daily.example: In Japan, soccer is as popular a sport as baseball.

daily.title: A travel guide
daily.description: Something you see when reading a guidebook.
daily.example: This hot spring is famous as one on a par with Kusatsu.

work.title: Economic news
work.description: Reporting an industry's standing.
work.example: Along with manufacturing, tourism supports the local economy.

work.title: Company introduction
work.description: Introducing core businesses in promotional material.
work.example: Our overseas business is a pillar of our company, on a par with our domestic business.

etymology: The basic meaning of 「並ぶ」 is “to line up, to be side by side”. From standing side by side in space, it came to mean being equal in standing or degree.

similar.title: 〜とともに
similar.explanation: 「とともに」 means “together with” or “as ... changes”, focusing on doing things together or changing at the same time. 「と並んで」 focuses on equal standing or degree.

similar.title: 〜をはじめ
similar.explanation: 「をはじめ」 uses the first item as a representative example of a group. 「と並んで」 puts two things on the same level.

similar.title: 〜に匹敵する
similar.explanation: 「に匹敵する」 means “to rival” in ability or scale. It's literary and stresses the comparison more. 「と並んで」 sounds milder.

title: 〜み (adjective → noun)
meaning: Added to the stem of some adjectives to make a noun for a quality, state, or feeling that you can sense.
connection: Stem of some i-adjectives・na-adjectives + み

senses.label: Taste／feel
senses.meaning: A quality you can sense by taste, touch, or sight, such as sweetness, bitterness, a reddish tint, or roundness.
senses.connection: 「甘み」, 「苦み」, 「辛み」, 「赤み」, 「丸み」, 「厚み」, etc.
examples: This tomato is very sweet.
I like the bitterness of coffee.
The corners in this design are rounded.

senses.label: Abstract qualities
senses.meaning: Abstract weight, depth, strengths, weaknesses, etc. Often used with 「ある」, 「増す」, or 「欠ける」.
senses.connection: 「重み」, 「深み」, 「強み」, 「弱み」, 「温かみ」, 「面白み」, etc.
examples: His words carry weight.
Her language skills are her strength.
Handwritten letters have a certain warmth.

senses.label: Feelings
senses.meaning: Inner feelings. Most of these have become fixed nouns.
senses.connection: 「楽しみ」, 「悲しみ」, 「ありがたみ」, 「親しみ」, 「苦しみ」, etc.
examples: I'm looking forward to next week's trip.
Only after losing them did I realize how precious my family was.

notes: 「み」 attaches only to certain adjectives; you can't make new words freely: ✕「大きみ」 ✕「新しみ」.
「さ」 shows a measurable degree (「重さ」 = weight), while 「み」 shows a quality you feel (「重み」 = weightiness, significance).
「楽しみ」, 「苦しみ」, etc. are also verb masu-stems. The 「み」 in 「楽しみます」 is not this grammar.

daily.title: At a meal
daily.description: Commenting on the taste of a dish with a friend.
daily.example: This soup isn't quite spicy enough, is it?

daily.title: Before a date
daily.description: Telling someone you're looking forward to it.
daily.example: I'm really looking forward to seeing you this weekend.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a character's sadness.
daily.example: Deep sorrow showed in her eyes.

work.title: A job interview
work.description: Talking about your strengths.
work.example: My strength is perseverance.

work.title: Product description
work.description: Describing a product's appeal.
work.example: Its charm is the warmth that only comes from being handmade by craftsmen.

etymology: The suffix 「み」 is thought to be related to an old 「み」 that showed a state (as in 「山高み」). After an adjective stem it means “the way that quality exists”. It's usually written in kana, but sometimes as 「味」, as in 「新鮮味」 or 「人間味」.

similar.title: 〜さ
similar.explanation: 「さ」 attaches to almost any adjective and shows an objective, measurable degree (「高さ」 = height). 「み」 attaches to only some adjectives and shows a quality you feel (「高み」 = a height, a high level).

similar.title: 〜っぽい
similar.explanation: 「っぽい」 makes an adjective meaning “-ish, like ...”. 「み」 makes a noun.

meaning: Partial negation: it's generally thought to be so, but it isn't always the case. Like “not necessarily ...”.
connection: 必ずしも + plain form + （わけでは）ない／とは限らない／とは言えない

senses.label: Not necessarily
senses.meaning: Denies “always, definitely” and allows for exceptions. Often followed by 「わけではない」 or 「とは言えない」. Objective and soft.
senses.connection: 必ずしも 〜ない／〜わけではない／〜とは言えない
examples: Expensive things aren't necessarily good.
You can't say that rich people are necessarily happy.

senses.label: Not always
senses.meaning: Most often paired with 「〜とは限らない」: “you can't say it's always so”. Often used to challenge common sense or general views.
senses.connection: 必ずしも plain form + とは限らない
examples: Experts' opinions aren't always right.
Working hard doesn't always mean you'll succeed.

notes: 「必ず」 means “definitely”, but 「必ずしも」 must pair with a negative to make a partial negation: ✕「必ずしも来る」.
Common in papers, news, and essays, but also fine in everyday speech.

daily.title: Discussing school choices
daily.description: Talking with family about top universities and happiness.
daily.example: Even if you get into a famous university, it doesn't mean you'll necessarily get a good job.

daily.title: Online reviews
daily.description: Warning a friend not to trust reviews blindly.
daily.example: A place with lots of reviews isn't necessarily good.

work.title: Discussion in a meeting
work.description: Politely offering a different opinion.
work.example: We can't say that past cases necessarily apply this time.

work.title: An academic paper
work.description: Pointing out that two things aren't necessarily cause and effect.
work.example: There is not necessarily a causal relationship between the two.

etymology: It's 「必ず」 (“definitely”) + the emphatic particle 「しも」. 「しも」 is an old emphatic particle that, with a negative, means “not all ...”, which gave the partial-negation meaning “not necessarily”.

similar.title: 〜とは限らない
similar.explanation: 「とは限らない」 alone already means “not necessarily”. Adding 「必ずしも」 makes the partial negation clearer, and the two are often used together.

similar.title: 〜わけではない
similar.explanation: 「わけではない」 denies a conclusion drawn from what came before. With 「必ずしも」, it means “it's not always the case”.

similar.title: 〜ないとも限らない
similar.explanation: 「ないとも限らない」 means “it's not impossible that ...” and points out a possibility. 「必ずしも〜ない」 denies that something is inevitable.

meaning: Denies the first item and gives the correct second one. Like “not A, but B”.
connection: Noun／na-adjective stem + ではなく（て）／じゃなくて; plain form + のではなく

senses.label: Not A but B
senses.meaning: Denies A and uses B to correct or explain the real situation. 「ではなく」 is more written; 「ではなくて」 is slightly more spoken.
senses.connection: Noun + ではなく（て）、B
examples: This isn't mine; it's my brother's.
Please contact me by email, not by phone.

senses.label: Spoken form
senses.meaning: 「じゃなくて」 is the spoken form and the most common in daily conversation. It can also be used on its own to correct what you just said.
senses.connection: Noun + じゃなくて、B
examples: I'll have tea, not coffee.
It's tomorrow, not today.

senses.label: Written／with verbs
senses.meaning: Verbs and adjectives use 「のではなく」. In writing you can drop 「は」 and say 「でなく」.
senses.connection: Plain form + のではなく; noun + でなく
examples: Instead of running away, you should face the problem.
What matters is not the result but the process.

notes: 「だけでなく」 and 「ばかりでなく」 mean “not only ... but also”, which is different.
「ではなくても」 and 「でなくてもいい」 mean “it's fine even if it isn't ...”. That's not this grammar.
Verbs can't attach directly: ✕「行くではなく」. Say 「行くのではなく」.

daily.title: Ordering food
daily.description: Correcting your order.
daily.example: Sorry, not iced. Hot, please.

daily.title: Clearing up a misunderstanding
daily.description: Explaining the real situation to a friend.
daily.example: I'm not angry, I'm just a bit tired.

work.title: Speaking at a meeting
work.description: Stressing the real goal.
work.example: What we're aiming for is not higher sales, but higher customer satisfaction.

work.title: A report
work.description: Explaining the cause of a problem.
work.example: The cause lies not in individual error, but in a flaw in the system.

etymology: It's made of 「で」 (the continuative form of 「だ」) + the topic particle 「は」 + 「なく」 (the continuative form of 「ない」). It is the linking form of 「ではない」. 「じゃ」 is a spoken contraction of 「では」.

similar.title: 〜じゃなくて〜（N5）
similar.explanation: At N5 you learn the basic spoken form. This entry adds the written 「ではなく」 and 「でなく」, and the use of 「のではなく」.

similar.title: 〜ばかりでなく
similar.explanation: 「ばかりでなく」 and 「だけでなく」 mean “not only A, but also B”: both A and B are true. With 「ではなく」, A is denied and only B is true.

similar.title: 〜代わりに
similar.explanation: 「代わりに」 means “instead of”: A and B are swapped. 「ではなく」 is a correction: A itself is denied.

meaning: Raises a question first, then answers it or denies it. Like “If you ask why ..., it's because ...” or “Does that mean ...? Not really.”
connection: Question word + plain form + かというと; plain form (nouns・na-adjectives may drop 「だ」) + かというと

senses.label: Asking and answering yourself
senses.meaning: Used with a question word: you raise a question, then give the answer or reason. Often paired with 「からだ」 or 「のだ」. Common in explanations.
senses.connection: Question word (なぜ・どうして・どこ, etc.) 〜かというと、〜からだ
examples: The reason I was late is that the train stopped.
Why did I choose this job? Because I wanted to help people.

senses.label: Denying an assumption
senses.meaning: Without a question word, it raises a view many people might hold, then denies it. The second part is often 「そうではない」 or 「そうとは限らない」.
senses.connection: Plain form + かというと、そうでもない／そうとは限らない
examples: Does having money make you happy? Not necessarily.
Are all Japanese people good at keigo? Not really.

senses.label: どちらかというと
senses.meaning: A set phrase meaning that, when comparing two things, you lean toward one. Also 「どちらかといえば」.
senses.connection: どちらかというと／どちらかといえば + judgment
examples: I'm more of a morning person.
If I had to choose, I prefer cats to dogs.

notes: 「かといって」 means “even so, (that doesn't mean) ...”, which is a different grammar point.
「〜かというと」 can also be 「〜かといえば」, which is slightly more formal.

daily.title: Explaining to a friend
daily.description: Giving the reason you moved.
daily.example: The reason I moved is that it's close to work.

daily.title: Talking about personality
daily.description: Describing your tendencies.
daily.example: I'm more the type who likes to spend time alone.

work.title: A speech or presentation
work.description: Posing a question, then explaining the reason.
work.example: Why did this product sell? Because it was reasonably priced.

work.title: An opinion piece
work.description: Denying a common view.
work.example: Will tighter regulation solve the problem? It's not that simple.

etymology: It's made of the question particle 「か」 + quoting 「と」 + 「言う」 + the conditional 「と」. Literally “if you say whether ...”, it's used to lead into the answer to a question.

similar.title: 〜というと
similar.explanation: 「というと」 brings up a topic or an association (“speaking of ...”). 「かというと」 raises a question and then answers or denies it.

similar.title: 〜かといって
similar.explanation: 「かといって」 means “even so, (that doesn't mean) ...” and is used for a contrast. 「かというと」 explains a reason or denies an assumption.

similar.title: なぜなら〜からだ
similar.explanation: 「なぜなら」 directly introduces the reason and is more literary. 「なぜ〜かというと」 restates the question first, then answers, sounding more conversational and well-organized.

title: 〜当たり (per)
meaning: Follows a number with a unit to mean “per ...” or “on average per ...”. Used to calculate rates and averages.
connection: Counter word (一人・1日・1時間, etc.) + 当たり／あたり

senses.label: Per unit
senses.meaning: Shows an average based on a certain unit. Often used for data like costs, output, or consumption. 「〜当たりの + noun」 modifies a noun.
senses.connection: Number + 人/個/台, etc. + 当たり（の）
examples: The cost is 3,000 yen per person.
Per-capita rice consumption in Japan is decreasing year by year.
This car gets 20 kilometers per liter.

senses.label: Per period of time
senses.meaning: After a time unit, shows an amount per unit of time. Often used for wages, speed, numbers of visitors, etc.
senses.connection: Number + 時間/日/か月, etc. + 当たり
examples: The hourly wage went up.
On average, 500 people visit this shop per day.

notes: 「日当たり」 (sunlight), 「人当たり」 (manner with people), and 「心当たり」 (an idea, a clue) are separate words, not this grammar.
「この辺り」 and 「駅のあたり」 mean “around here／near the station”, which is also not this grammar.
In speech people usually say 「一人あたり」; formal documents usually write 「当たり」.

daily.title: Splitting the bill
daily.description: Working out how much each person pays.
daily.example: It's 10,000 yen in total, so that's 2,500 yen each.

daily.title: Looking for a part-time job
daily.description: Comparing hourly pay with a friend.
daily.example: How much does this job pay per hour?

work.title: Economic news
work.description: Reporting per-capita income data.
work.example: Per-capita GDP exceeded the previous year's.

work.title: Cost calculation
work.description: Calculating unit cost in a report.
work.example: We need to reduce the cost per product.

etymology: 「当たり」 is the noun form of the verb 「当たる」 (“to correspond; to be allotted”). It means “the share allotted to ...”, and from that, “per ...”.

similar.title: 〜ずつ
similar.explanation: 「ずつ」 means dividing evenly or the same amount each time (「一人二個ずつ」). 「当たり」 shows a rate or average based on a unit.

similar.title: 〜につき
similar.explanation: 「につき」 can also mean “per” (「一人につき千円」). It's more formal and used for rules and fees. 「当たり」 is used more for statistics and calculations.

similar.title: 〜ごとに
similar.explanation: 「ごとに」 means “every ...”, focusing on something happening repeatedly. 「当たり」 focuses on an average amount.
